power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

info.title: The Arena Model An Account of Human Judgment

text.text: Psychology, economics, and behavioral science catalog human judgment through hundreds of disparate cognitive biases.
The Arena Model (AM) replaces this disjointed taxonomy with a single account: judgment runs on a low-dimensional projection of a higher-dimensional world.
The model derives many canonical heuristics and biases from a few fixed mechanisms.

A "bias," per the AM account, is what happens when a mind works with fewer dimensions than its environment contains, when a researcher measures dimensions that differ from what the mind used, or when an internal signal is taken to report a property of the world.
Many apparent departures from rationality resolve once unmeasured and mismatched dimensions are taken into account.

Unlike descriptive frameworks that add a new mechanism for each phenomenon, the AM constrains the space of possible errors and yields clear, falsifiable predictions about the conditions under which biases will and will not appear.
It also gives researchers a single, testable account in place of a growing list of unconnected exceptions.
I demonstrate consistency across known biases, define the limits of the account, and propose a diagnostic test to evaluate, or invalidate, it.
Expansive volumes of research catalog how human judgment deviates from normative models [72, 27].
text.formatted: Expansive volumes of research catalog how human judgment deviates from normative models <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">[72,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">27]</ref>.

text.text: Unifying accounts of judgment are much rarer.

The Arena Model (AM) addresses this gap by treating judgment as systematic motion through a high-dimensional space (the arena), with biases arising from misinterpretations or violations of that space.
Fields fill the arena, but they only describe the space.
What acts on the fields to form judgments, and what gets left out when they are read, are what generate the heuristics and biases documented by the judgment and decision making (JDM) catalog.
The meat and drink of the AM is that catalog.

It is a monumental empirical achievement that impresses equally with its hundreds of named, many of which are replicated, departures from normative standards and the cleverness of empirical manipulations that isolate them.
A result of remarkable enthusiasm for JDM science, it is now a catalog of overwhelming size that forfeits the very clarity its entries are meant to provide.
Each entry functions as a primitive explanandum, separate from any shared, more basic derivation.
Relatedly, JDM models are frequently simplified to a degree that undermines their descriptive abilities.
Real sources of variance are absorbed into "noise," not directly modeled [43].
text.formatted: Real sources of variance are absorbed into "noise," not directly modeled <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">[43]</ref>.

text.text: The AM account is, among other things, a proposal about where some of that variance lives.
It is not an editorial correction to the catalog, nor is it an argument for how to accomplish that process.
It is a reframing of how we think about judgment that forces a reconciling of the JDM catalog.
Situating the AM account against what its neighbors already supply will make its committed divergences more intelligible.
Lewin's psychological field theory [45] claims that human behavior is the result of interacting psychological forces within and across a person's total psychological environment.
text.formatted: Lewin's psychological field theory <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">[45]</ref> claims that human behavior is the result of interacting psychological forces within and across a person's total psychological environment.

text.text: A fundamental difference between the two accounts is that fields alone do not constitute the AM.
The model only becomes a meaningful theory under the weight of its defined operations, functionals, and equipment.
They are what afford the AM its ability to recover catalog entries and predict the conditions under which new anomalies should appear.
The heuristics-and-biases tradition supplies the catalog and much of the observational vocabulary this paper works from.
The named entries, their manipulations, and the standards against which they are scored can all be traced to this tradition [72].
text.formatted: The named entries, their manipulations, and the standards against which they are scored can all be traced to this tradition <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">[72]</ref>.

text.text: The AM account differs by declining to take those entries as primitive.
It treats them as explananda for derivation, not as the theoretical bedrock.

The adaptive-toolbox and ecological-rationality traditions supply the insight that apparently poor judgment is often well-adapted to the statistics of a real environment, and that a standard can itself be mismatched to the task [27].
text.formatted: The adaptive-toolbox and ecological-rationality traditions supply the insight that apparently poor judgment is often well-adapted to the statistics of a real environment, and that a standard can itself be mismatched to the task <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">[27]</ref>.

text.text: The AM concedes that insight for one class of phenomena ( §2.5), but does not extend it to the whole catalog.
Decision Field Theory supplies a dynamic, formal account of deliberation.
It is an explicit process model of how preference accumulates over the course of a single choice [10].
text.formatted: It is an explicit process model of how preference accumulates over the course of a single choice <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10]</ref>.

text.text: The AM operates at a more fundamental level: it models the substrate that generates the ensemble of episodes deliberation draws from.
The AM also differs from quantum cognition, which supplies a formalism flexible enough to fit a wide range of observed anomalies, including order effects and violations of classical probability [9].
text.formatted: The AM also differs from quantum cognition, which supplies a formalism flexible enough to fit a wide range of observed anomalies, including order effects and violations of classical probability <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9]</ref>.

text.text: Where the quantum cognition approach is to accommodate anomalies through formal flexibility, the AM seeks to derive them from a compact parameter set.
Free-energy and active-inference accounts supply a top-down governing principle for cognition and action: the minimization of surprise or prediction error [23].
text.formatted: Free-energy and active-inference accounts supply a top-down governing principle for cognition and action: the minimization of surprise or prediction error <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">[23]</ref>.

text.text: The AM takes the opposite formal direction and serves a different purpose: it starts from primitives and builds upward, yielding a generative capability that produces testable predictions ( §3.5).
An architecture that runs upward is the core structural commitment of the AM.
Model primitives generate composites, and composites (in some cases, the primitives directly) generate the JDM catalog phenomena.
Everything that follows executes this claim.
Section 3 establishes the AM functionally, from its primitives through to the composites assembled from them.
Section 4 demonstrates how catalog phenomena are derived from, not posited by, the AM.
Section 5 shows what the AM account forbids.
Most substantively, transformations along dimensions not recruited for a judgment are predicted to leave it unchanged.
Accepting the primitives implies a commitment to what follows from them.
Voicing a doubt about the AM explaining a downstream phenomenon requires pointing to which primitive or composite the doubt strains.
The upward trajectory of the AM, from primitives to phenomena, is an essential support of its judgment reframing.
Section 2 provides an intuitive introduction of the upward perspective.
Under this interpretation, a bias is often what a hidden dimension looks like when seen from a projection that lacks it.
The model's formalism makes the reframe more than just a metaphor.

The arena, its fields, and the operations that act on them translate the metaphor into a derivable consequence of how a person's judgment is confined to a lowerdimensional slice of the arena (Def. 3.3).
text.formatted: The arena, its fields, and the operations that act on them translate the metaphor into a derivable consequence of how a person's judgment is confined to a lowerdimensional slice of the arena (Def. <ref type="bibr">3.3</ref>).

text.text: An object earns its place in the AM account by compression, or how much of the JDM catalog it collapses, weighed against what it costs to posit.
Objects are not admitted for correspondence to any neural or computational structure (made precise in §3).
They allow the AM to describe what is computed, and under what constraints, such that cataloged phenomena follow.
Accordingly, it makes descriptive claims.
Prescriptive applications may follow as downstream consequences.
For example, knowing what generates a bias identifies a potential target for intervention.
Rationality axioms and similar normative frameworks of idealized behavior enter as external overlays on the machinery for naming deviations.
The AM account is an invitation to anyone interested in gaining insight into the JDM catalog.
It invites readers to trace individual entries to common foundational elements.
The procedure in Appendix A outlines how to apply the AM.
My hope is that readers will run it: take an entry, locate the signal being read and what it is read as, trace it to its primitive(s), and press on the result.
I expect it to fail in places, as the opacity of human thought all but guarantees that specific model mechanics will break down.
Yet the underlying concept remains sound: build from primitives, establish composites, and generate predictions.
This process is a departure from the historical JDM route of proposing a mechanism, developing a manipulation, and reporting a difference.
That process leaves null results ambiguous; the approach I take with the AM generates clearly falsifiable predictions ranging from specific gaps in the catalog to the AM itself.
The core AM claim is that judgment is systematic motion along recruited dimensions in a multidimensional space, or arena, that decisions range over.
It is composed of fields, or quantities that are defined at every point in the space, much like there is a temperature at every point in a room.
Human judgment is capacity-limited [65, 14], meaning people cannot consider their judgment arena in its entirety.
text.formatted: Human judgment is capacity-limited <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">[65,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">14]</ref>, meaning people cannot consider their judgment arena in its entirety.

text.text: The AM represents that limitation by requiring judgment to operate on a low-dimensional projection of the arena.
A person must establish a working arena, the projection, by selecting a basis, the few dimensions they recruit from the arena, to form judgments.
Researchers face a similar limitation.
Empirical constraints force them to measure low-dimensional projections of a person's judgments.
Two options that appear identical in the projection they have selected may be genuinely different points in the full judgment arena.
A projection is a choice of coordinates, and a coordinate is a dimension together with an origin and a scale.
Thus, two options can differ within a projection in three ways -along a dimension the experimenter did not measure, in the position of an origin, or in scale.
Observed inconsistencies can become projection artifacts under this claim.
To illustrate, consider a circular shadow cast on a wall.
The shadow reveals neither the source object (a sphere, a cylinder, or a flat disc?), its exact position relative to the light, nor its absolute scale.
Inferring a person's true judgment from an empirical projection is like identifying the object from its shadow.
This is the projection view of biases.
Consider framing.
The invariance axiom asserts that description-change is identity-preserving.
Framing the projected death rate of a disease around the number of people saved, versus the number of deaths, should not alter a judgment [73].
text.formatted: Framing the projected death rate of a disease around the number of people saved, versus the number of deaths, should not alter a judgment <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">[73]</ref>.

text.text: This axiom is a transformation of the decision situation that should leave judgment unchanged.

However, if description-change moves judgment -by recruiting a dimension the axiom ignored, or by relocating the origin the outcome is read against -then the axiom is false about the arena, not violated by the system. "90% survival" and "10% mortality" coincide only in an experimenter's projection.
We perceive familiar objects as having stable, unchanging properties [8].
text.formatted: We perceive familiar objects as having stable, unchanging properties <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8]</ref>.

text.text: I perceive an approaching friend as retaining a stable size across changes in distance, viewing angle, and lighting.
It is tempting to draw the analogy that rationality axioms are the JDM constancies and biases are their failures.
However, this analogy fails because it requires a distal invariant like a property, characteristic, or structure that the judgment process is trying to recover.
My friend -I swear I have one -is really out there.
My perceptual system inverts an ecologically limited generative model to give meaning to failure: there was a right answer that context either aided or did not.
For much of judgment, recovery lacks a distal invariant.
A newly minted mug owner's willingnessto-accept is not recovering an invariant fact about the mug, nor is a potential buyer's willingness-to-pay missing one [41].
text.formatted: A newly minted mug owner's willingnessto-accept is not recovering an invariant fact about the mug, nor is a potential buyer's willingness-to-pay missing one <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">[41]</ref>.

text.text: Judgment-as-estimation is the narrow exception to this interpretation, as it often focuses on real quantities with ground truths.
But many catalog entries, such as framing, preference reversal, and intransitivity, follow the rule and are what the projection view dissolves.
The JDM catalog entries are essential empirical anchor points.
They lend valuable insight into human behavior, particularly when a decision necessitates understanding population-level tendencies.
Moreover, for present purposes, every documented anomaly in the JDM catalog points at the dimension(s) it reveals.
Framing, for example, provides charted coordinates in the nominal dimensions of "reference" and "pragmatics" (speaker's emphasis).
Under the projection view, those coordinates are a point in the judgment arena where Tversky and Kahneman noticed an intelligible projection.

Framing a disease as having a 90% survival rate relies on the interpreter's reference value for what constitutes a good rate while glossing over the speaker's persuasion intentions.

text.text: The JDM community recognizes that the endowment effect emerges from the act of sliding along a dimension collapsed by its projection.
The dispute, then, is less about whether valuation gaps arise than about what generates them.
Each advance researchers make in this debate uncovers new coordinates of the effect, helping the discipline accurately place it in the judgment arena.
I interpret it as evidence of the projection view doing work long before it was named.
Importantly, those coordinates reveal judgment dimensions for the arena model to capture.
To study the endowment effect, framing, or any other bias, a researcher must select a basis, the truncated set of judgment dimensions.
Any observed judgment, under the projection view, is a higher-dimensional process seen by the experimenter as a low-dimensional projection across their chosen dimensions.
The same is true for their participants.
When faced with a judgment, a person must instantiate their working arena, a similarly low-dimensional projection that is cue-driven from slow, accumulated structure.
The endowment effect literature is evidence of researchers iteratively attempting to calibrate their projections to the projections of subjects.
Many biases are found in the delta between experimenter and participant projections.
When a participant moves through their working arena during a judgment, misalignment between the participant's and experimenter's projections hides part of the participant's path.
When the path trace leaves the experimenter's projection, trying to reconcile it with the assumed basis can result in the path looking unpredictable, even irrational.
The original endowment effect experiment worked because the experimental procedure demanded a particular basis from the participants and that basis was misaligned with the hypothesized basis.
The conversation that has transpired in the literature since the original publication, when viewed through the projection view lens, is a discussion around aligning those bases.

Each iterative pass has altered the endowment effect's coordinates, either by unlocking a new judgment dimension or by showing how the judgment was stable in the experimental basis, but moving elsewhere.
An experimenter's selection of a basis is ordinary dimensionality reduction, which makes an empirical question tractable by supplying a reference for comparison.
Here, the term projection refers specifically to that reduction and carries no assumption that unmeasured alternatives interact.
This process and the discovered insights provide a firm foundation for deriving a generative model capable of uncovering what may be occurring in the collapsed dimensions of a judgment projection.
The obvious risk of a modeling paradigm that posits dimensions to explain observed variance, versus strictly stating what dimensions are under consideration, is proliferation.
Any inconsistency is quickly explained by simply adding another dimension to the model.

This was the fault in Ptolemy's stars: whenever astronomers observed celestial bodies moving contrary to what his base model predicted, they simply added more epicycles instead of scrapping the original model [44].
text.formatted: This was the fault in Ptolemy's stars: whenever astronomers observed celestial bodies moving contrary to what his base model predicted, they simply added more epicycles instead of scrapping the original model <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">[44]</ref>.

text.text: For the AM, proliferation strips it of its utility as a compact, generative tool and forces it to compete with other anomaly-explaining approaches, such as quantum cognition.
Guarding against this risk means treating a dimension and an origin as what they are: two different components of a coordinate (Def.
3.3), each having its own criterion.

A dimension earns admission by being independently measurable and doing work across many phenomena; a hidden axis invoked to save a single anomaly, and never checked against any other case, has not met this bar.
An origin does not add an axis, only relocates the zero already attached to a recruited one.
The AM subjects origins to a narrower discipline while dimensions face the cross-phenomenon requirement above.

An origin shift becomes an epicycle when the origin move cannot be traced to something the person plausibly had to compare against (recent experience, a salient anchor, a typical case, or an expected outcome) and is posited only because it rescues the result.
Note that scale is different in that pure rescaling leaves judgment unchanged ( §3), excluding it as an explanation for an anomaly.
The rules above discipline how a dimension or origin may be posited.
They leave open the separate question of which biases warrant reaching for one in the first place.
Not every bias or apparent inconsistency in judgment is mismeasured rational behavior.
The projection view addresses a particular class of observed biases characterized by hidden-dimension artifacts; framing and the endowment effect are the standard cases of this class.
Their documented inconsistencies, I argue, arise when the experimenter's projection obscures the participant's movement along the hidden dimension(s).
The projection view lets us predict and explain this class of biases from the JDM catalog.
At least two additional classes fall outside the projection view.
The first consists of capacity and noise limits.
As Herbert Simon famously noted, humans are boundedly rational [65].
text.formatted: As Herbert Simon famously noted, humans are boundedly rational <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">[65]</ref>.

text.text: Our brains have finite processing capacity, information is almost always incomplete, and we frequently face strict time constraints, all of which hinder our ability to fully engage with a judgment.
When a person loses track of their early reasoning steps during a judgment under load, the judgment may not move systematically along an unmeasured dimension.
Losing those early steps is an actual failure.
As will be made clear, the AM handles this class of failures with machinery for capacity-and decay-imposed limitations.
A second class consists of ecological adaptations: behavior suited to environmental statistics but scored against a mismatched standard [27].
text.formatted: A second class consists of ecological adaptations: behavior suited to environmental statistics but scored against a mismatched standard <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">[27]</ref>.

text.text: Because these are overlay problems, they do not dissolve under the projection view and the account concedes them as outside its purview.

The AM dissolves the hidden-dimension class of biases, handles capacityand noise-based biases via its machinery, and generally concedes that many, such as those explained by ecological adaptations, are outside its purview.
The projection view holds that a judgment relies entirely on the dimensions recruited as its working arena.
A transformation affecting an unrecruited dimension will not impact the judgment.
This premise lets the theory derive invariances of judgment by identifying conditions under which biases should not appear.
This approach is not the first to derive predictions from theory.

For example, evidence supporting the argument that human cognition is best adapted to natural frequencies followed from formal predictions that stated aligning statistical information with such an adaptation would help people solve associated problems [13, 28].

text.text: Seen from the AM perspective, a format change represents a coordinate re-encoding within the same dimensional space, and a format effect is not a true invariance.
The projection view claim goes beyond boundary conditions to establish dynamics in which judgment remains constant despite underlying dimensional shifts.
The arena model generates invariance predictions across the JDM catalog because the core question that it asks -which dimensions constitute the working arena? -is portable to every entry.
The typical process of making a new JDM catalog entry is to propose a mechanism, find a manipulation, and report a difference.
That process has produced a legion of valuable behavioral insight; however, ambiguity characterizes its null results.
Researchers are left with the task of determining whether a null result was from incorrect operationalization of the theorized mechanism, a lack of power for the manipulation, or the wrong stimulus.
In contrast, the projection view shifts its gaze from predicting behavioral effects to invariances.
This shift facilitates a different type of behavioral science, but comes with its own demands and risks.
First, it requires committing to which dimensions a person recruits during the judgment under scrutiny.
Second, a transformation must be identified that leaves what the judgment reads untouched.
Shifting a dimension into play or relocating a reference the judgment is read against is not allowed.
Section 3 makes those two requirements precise once the necessary machinery has been laid out.
That commitment is the sword that the AM lives and dies by.

Because the requirements are stated in terms of the dimensions a person recruits, a failed invariance can always be explained after the fact by asserting that the transformation must have violated one of them.

To rule this out, both the recruitment claim and the neutrality of the transformation must be committed to in advance, on grounds independent of the result they are used to predict (the same discipline imposed on dimensions in §2.5).
A transformation argued to be neutral only after the invariance failed is not evidence for the account; it is the epicycle the projection view exists to avoid.
When a preregistered invariance does fail, the honest reading is that the posited working arena, the posited reference, or the transformation was wrong.
The AM account is designed to say where to look first during failure diagnostics.
For a practical illustration, consider the account's separation of attribute framing from valence framing.
Highlighting an apartment's air conditioning or its distance from a busy street is pure basis selection.
Highlighting one changes which dimensions enter the working arena.
Gain-and-loss wording works differently.

"Save $100 a month compared to the median rent" and "lose $100 a month by renting elsewhere" invoke the same dimension (monthly cost) but imply different reference points, so the origin moves while the arena stays put.
The AM prediction follows directly: a paraphrase that changes neither the dimensions in play nor the implied reference should not have an effect.
Wording matters when it recruits a dimension or relocates an origin; otherwise, it does not.
The distinction casts new light on the canonical framing demonstration.
One minus survival is mortality, a single dimension described from opposite sides.
The manipulation reverses the dimension in play, but critically, reversing an axis relocates its origin to the opposite end.
Orientation and origin move together.
The original study was not designed to separate such mechanisms, but to demonstrate the framing effect.
That being said, the field's most-cited framing result cannot isolate an orientation from an origin manipulation.
Testing them requires cases that manipulate one while holding the other fixed.
The arena model has three layers.
Primitives are the irreducible components of judgment: the space over which it ranges, the fields defined on that space, and the settings a person brings to it.
Composites are assembled from primitives, and are where observed biases originate.
Phenomena are the entries of the JDM catalog; they are what we measure, name, and argue over.
Four terms I rely on deserve defining.
Primitives generate a signal: they are the machinery that produces it.
A readout takes a quantity as input: it operatively depends on that quantity, and only what a readout takes as input can move a judgment.
A derivation invokes a quantity when it names that quantity in explaining a phenomenon.
It may invoke quantities outside the agent's operative input, including the reading warranted by a standard.
An overlay, like a rationality axiom, scores a judgment against an external yardstick.
That yardstick remains external to the machinery.
Two pairs also deserve defining.

A judgment's warranted signal is the quantity the standard it is scored against would require; its operative signal is the quantity it actually goes on, which is to say the quantity its readout takes as input.
The two often coincide (Appendix A).
A misreading is then a fact about a trace: the operative signal is taken to report something it does not report.
An error is a verdict, returned when a judgment is scored.
A misreading gets no verdict in the absence of an applicable standard, and a judgment can be scored an error with no misreading in it, as when capacity truncates a sample.
Primitives earn their keep by compressing an otherwise overwhelming catalog of ideas.
Composite-level description remains useful after compression to primitives.
Although protons are made of quarks, nuclear chemistry is done in protons.
Salience, according to the AM, is a composite like a proton.
Behavioral science, like nuclear chemistry, operates at that level.
The primitives explain why composites exist and how they can be perturbed, while composites are what we model higher-order phenomena with.
The AM is at Marr's computational level [50].

text.text: It specifies what is computed and under what constraints, leaving algorithms and physical realization open.
This commitment has three consequences.
First, functional role defines each object.
Second, accuracy, coherence, and consistency characterize judgment outcomes; the machinery itself implements no normative standard.
Third, each object receives a signature and boundary conditions, while algorithmic accounts supply the functional forms.
Definition 3.1 (Equipped arena).
The equipped arena is Σ = ( 𝒳, 𝑤, 𝐷 ), where 𝒳 is the arena, 𝑤 ∶ 𝒳 × 𝒳 → ℝ ≥0 is the cost function, and 𝐷 ∶ 𝒳 → ℝ ≥0 is trace-density.
The arena is a product of 𝑁 ordered coordinate axes, each an interval of ℝ, carrying a reference measure with respect to which the integrals below are taken.
The equipped arena sets the stage with the AM's required elements, which are tackled as the build requires.
The reference measure is what enables a field to be integrated over the arena.
The account's central functionals, the capacity constraint (Def.
3.6) and the entropy of a field (end of this subsection), are of this kind.
The coordinates are ordered because a coordinate is a dimension given an origin and a scale (Def.
3.3), and a scale presupposes order.
Because coordinates presuppose order, the model represents categorical structure as regions.
The product structure makes marginalization, and in consequence projection onto a subset of coordinates, well defined.
𝑁 is finite because the claim that judgment runs in fewer dimensions than the arena is fundamentally a claim about counts.
Over the timescales addressed by the AM, 𝑁 remains fixed.
Expertise accumulates trace-density along an existing dimension and thereby changes the basis.
Learning to taste tannin separately from acidity in wine illustrates such a change.
Fixing 𝑁 prevents the arena from absorbing any anomaly through dimensional expansion.
That would conceal a proliferation risk within the model's machinery and undermine my falsifiability commitment ( §2.5).
The equipped arena names what the space carries and the record of where the system has been.
On its own, the arena is a collection of points.
Equipping it with 𝑤 and 𝐷 provides interpretive structure required for judgment to happen.
Substrate refers to the whole layer below the ceiling ( §3.4), of which the equipped arena is the spatial part.

text.text: Definition 3.4 (Possibility field).

The possibility field 𝐸 ∶ 𝒳 × 𝑇 × 𝐵 × Π → ℝ ≥0 , written 𝐸(𝑥 | 𝜏, 𝛽, 𝜋): a distribution over states, indexed by their displacement from the agent's own present, where: • 𝜏 ∈ 𝑇 is a temporal index parameterizing past vs. future extension; • 𝛽 ∈ 𝐵 is a branch index parameterizing actual vs. counterfactual alternatives; • 𝜋 ∈ Π is a perspective index parameterizing self vs. other positioning.
The null displacement (now, actual, self) is admissible; 𝐸 at that index is what discrepancy compares against the actuality field ( §3.3).
Displacement away from it is what makes the field a field of possibility rather than a second copy of the present.

Masses are therefore comparable within an index and not across indices; no readout in this account compares them across indices.

Because E2 permits non-zero mass without input support, 𝐸 generates predictions without needing external input.
Pattern detection in noise and spontaneous anticipation are structural consequences of this same generative support.
The actuality field 𝑆 ∶ 𝒳 → ℝ ≥0 : the agent's representation of the current state.
It carries no indices, being by construction 𝜏 = now, 𝛽 = actual, 𝜋 = self -and it is from 𝑆 that the indices of 𝐸 displace.
It is in this sense the account's basepoint: the here, now, and me relative to which everything else is elsewhere, later, otherwise, or someone.
𝑆 can be wrong, is held with uncertainty, and is entirely internal.
S2 (uncertainty type) 𝑆 is a field instead of an index position on 𝐸 because 𝐻[𝑆] is epistemic and reducible by information-seeking, while 𝐻[𝐸] is at least partly aleatory [22].
text.formatted: S2 (uncertainty type) 𝑆 is a field instead of an index position on 𝐸 because 𝐻[𝑆] is epistemic and reducible by information-seeking, while 𝐻[𝐸] is at least partly aleatory <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">[22]</ref>.

text.text: S3 (distinct dynamics) 𝑆 is written by input through the gate operation (Def.
3.10); 𝐸 is generated and updated by discrepancy.
S4 (no decay; the writer changes) 𝑆 is continuously written and does not decay.
With the gate open, input writes it; with the gate closed, 𝐸 writes it.
S5 (two readings) 𝑆 is read twice, each independent.
Marginalizing through 𝑃 𝑋 discards the dimensions along which 𝑆 is diffuse, leaving 𝑆 𝑋 .
The basepoint is a point-valued functional of 𝑆 𝑋 , while 𝐻[𝑆] is read separately as epistemic width (S2).
𝑆 may accordingly be broad while the basepoint is definite.
This is the same pattern as 𝐸, which yields mass, first moment, and spread to three different uses (two in Def.
3.14 and one in §3.7).
The basepoint is what cost-balls are measured from (Σ2).
It is not an origin in the sense of X1 because an origin fixes the zero of one coordinate, whereas the basepoint locates the space.
Because it is point-valued, ball membership, and therefore region membership (Def.
3.2), is crisp.
Current-state uncertainty is carried by 𝐻[𝑆] and does not blur which region a content falls in.
S7 (normalization) ∫ 𝒳 𝑆(𝑥) 𝑑𝑥 = 1.
𝐻[𝑆] in S2 is well defined because 𝑆 is a distribution over states, not an activation level.
Definition 3.6 (Capacity and activation).
Capacity 𝐾 ∈ ℝ + is a scalar reservoir and activation 𝐴 ∶ 𝒳 → ℝ ≥0 its allocation.
Let ‖𝐴‖ 𝐾 ∶= ∫ 𝒳 max(𝐴(𝑥) -𝜃, 0) 𝑑𝑥 for the draw of an allocation, where 𝜃 is the threshold above which content becomes available to the operations of §3.3.
The constraint is ‖𝐴‖ 𝐾 ≤ 𝐾, and ‖𝐴| 𝑅 ‖ 𝐾 denotes the draw restricted to a region 𝑅.
Only the mass above threshold is priced: content between 𝐷 and 𝜃 is elevated and decaying but free (K5).
Here 𝜃 is a uniform functional parameter.

Deriving it, for example, from a noise model which would require precision-limited discrimination against 𝐷, would make it location-dependent (𝜃 = 𝜃(𝑥)) and predict poorer source monitoring for familiar content.
I keep it uniform for simplicity.
The constraint is on mass, not cardinality.
K2 (allocation is not outcome) 𝐴 buys candidacy and resolution -which candidates are evaluated, and how finely.
Candidacy is being above 𝜃; resolution is sampling depth, the number of draws taken before a readout, which is one of the three ways deliberation spends 𝐾 ( §4.4).
Neither determines which candidate wins; 𝑔 does (Def.
K3 (two draws) Capacity is spent in two ways.
Traversal is priced by 𝑤: moving from one content to another incurs the cost specified by the cost function.
Maintenance is priced by duration of hold: the instantaneous price is the draw of the region held, ‖𝐴| 𝑅 ‖ 𝐾 , termed rent throughout.
Integrated over its duration, rent is capacity-time committed to the held region and unavailable elsewhere, against a fixed 𝐾.
Rent is measured in capacity units; valence is a separate kind of reading.

K4 (scalar with dimension-specific spend) 𝐾 is shared, while the numerator of felt-effort is dimension-specific spend over remaining capacity, hence domain-specific felt-effort without a vector budget.
K5 (decay) Unsupported 𝐴 decays toward 𝐷.
Content between 𝐷 and 𝜃 remains elevated and decaying while drawing zero capacity from 𝐾.
Heuristics, under this account, are a consequence of capacity pricing.
If computation were free, judgment could always derive an analytical solution and would never substitute a faster or more frugal process.
Definition 3.7 (Drive-gain).

The drive-gain field 𝑔 assigns to each direction of 𝒳 a signed gain that may vary with position along that direction: 𝑔 = (𝑔 1 , … , 𝑔 𝑁 ), where each 𝑔 𝑖 ∶ ℝ → ℝ takes the position 𝑥 𝑖 along coordinate 𝑖 to a signed gain 𝑔 𝑖 (𝑥 𝑖 ). 𝑔 𝑋 denotes its restriction to the recruited coordinates of a working arena.
A constant 𝑔 𝑖 is the ordinary case and the one most of the account operates in; the field form is what permits a gain to reverse across a dimension (G2).
The scalar 𝛾 that sets recruitment breadth (X3) is not a component of 𝑔: it governs how many coordinates are recruited, whereas 𝑔 weights what is read on the ones that are.
G1 (sign is primitive) sign(𝑔 𝑖 ) is not derivable from 𝐸, which is descriptive; from unsigned magnitude, which cannot flip; or from comparison, which yields sign only relative to a standard.
A sign boundary is a position 𝑥 * 𝑖 at which 𝑔 𝑖 changes sign.
Where mass sits at or across such a boundary, the contribution of coordinate 𝑖 to the valence profile (Def.
3.14) does not pass smoothly through zero: concentrated mass crossing 𝑥 * 𝑖 reverses that contribution, while distributed mass yields a reading that is continuous but non-differentiable at 𝑥 * 𝑖 .
Sharp reversal and a kink are thus the same fact at two levels of concentration, not two mechanisms.
Drive-gain is a sign-carrying dispositional setting, the irreducible protovalue that attaches to a dimension, and the quantity states can be more or less of.
Two quantities are read off it: stakes (G3) and valence (Def.
Read out over candidates, valence becomes value in the ordinary and economic sense.
The two words name one quantity; valence the signed reading, value what that reading is taken to be.
Scale is distinct from gain: scale is the unit of a coordinate and multiplies positions, whereas gain multiplies contributions to a readout.
So, two people may share a coordinate system and differ entirely in gain.
When an origin and a scale are selected for a dimension, it becomes a coordinate.
Because a coordinate requires an origin and a scale, every coordinate is ordered.
Categorical structure enters the account as regions, specifically cells crossed with cost-balls (S6).
Coordinates are constructed for each judgment by sampling slow structure under a cue.
From this follow two distinct focus-narrowing effects, acting at different stages.
Elevated 𝛾 concentrates recruitment over fewer dimensions when the working arena is spawned, capturing physiological arousal narrowing breadth (X3).
Once the arena is fixed, high stakes pull the capacity budget toward gainweighted coordinates, which is a second narrowing, for a different reason and within a basis already set.
That ordering ensures the account stays non-circular: because stakes is defined on the already-recruited coordinates (G3), it can drive allocation without helping to choose them.

Because 𝛾 and ‖ ḡ‖ dissociate (G4), the two narrowings do not need to coincide: the model predicts that an arousal manipulation, such as caffeine, narrows without raising stakes; a calm expert carries stakes without arousal narrowing.
The classic arousal-narrowing result [19] is the 𝛾 route.

text.text: Eight operations act on the fields defined above.
Two are distinguished by a load-bearing difference in arity: compare takes a candidate and a standard, whereas coherence takes a set of arbitrary size.
The structural limitations of compare warrant the 𝑚-ary form of coherence.
Definition 3.8 (Compare-to-standard). compare 𝑖 ∶ (candidate, standard) → ℝ, returning the signed difference along coordinate 𝑖 between the candidate and the standard.

Each operand is read on 𝑖 as a position: a point-valued operand supplies its own, and a field-valued operand supplies the first moment of its marginal on 𝑖, which is the same reading valence takes (Def.
The standard is that coordinate's origin (X1), except in discrepancy, in which case the standard is the actuality field.
Discrepancy is the case compare 𝑖 (𝐸(⋅ | now, actual, self), 𝑆).
The predictiveprocessing and reinforcement-learning literatures call this case "prediction error" [23, 15].
text.formatted: The predictiveprocessing and reinforcement-learning literatures call this case "prediction error" <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">[23,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">15]</ref>.

text.text: I use discrepancy throughout, because prediction is one regime of the possibility field, not a separate faculty.
The simultaneous requirement for two operands forces Definition 3.5.
Because compare is indexed, discrepancy is a profile over the recruited coordinates, not a single number.
When a scalar is wanted, as in salience recruitment ( §3.7), it is the norm of that profile.
The same holds of progress (Def.
3.15), which is compare against a clamped region.
Definition 3.9 (Coherence). coherence ∶ {𝑥 1 , … , 𝑥 𝑚 } → ℝ, returning a scalar fit over a set of co-active contents.
It takes no standard, is symmetric under permutation, is not defined relative to a dimension, and its value is unsigned.
Compare-to-standard returns a signed difference along a single coordinate, so it represents the relative positions of a candidate and standard on that axis.
That functionality makes dissonance unreachable for it.
"I am honest" and "I lied" are not incommensurable because both concern the self and honesty.
The compare operator would happily place them at different points on an honesty axis, losing information about how the latter is evidence against the former.
The coherence operation captures this relation by evaluating a set of arbitrary size and returning an unsigned fit independently of any dimension or standard.
Definition 3.10 (Gate).
The coupling from input to 𝑆.
Open: 𝑆 tracks input.
Closed: 𝑆 is decoupled from input and writable by 𝐸.

Definition 3.11 (Clamp). clamp ∶ (𝐸, 𝑅) → 𝐸, the restriction of 𝐸 to a region 𝑅, either input-driven (via the gate, not under allocation control) or allocationdriven (held by 𝐴, and so drawing rent ‖𝐴| 𝑅 ‖ 𝐾 for as long as it is held).
An admissible clamp satisfies 𝐻[clamp (𝐸, 𝑅)] ≤ 𝐻 [𝐸].
text.formatted: An admissible clamp satisfies 𝐻[clamp (𝐸, 𝑅)] ≤ 𝐻 <ref type="bibr">[𝐸]</ref>.

text.text: The entropy condition is a constraint on admissible forms, not a theorem.
Conditioning on a specific region can actually increase entropy, as when a sharply peaked field is restricted to a broad, flat region.
Only the average over conditioning events is guaranteed to be non-increasing.
Requiring the inequality is what makes clamping the entropy-reducing direction, against which update (Def.
3.12) is the entropy-permitting one.
Definition 3.12 (Update).
On discrepancy, 𝐸 moves toward 𝑆 with precisionweighted gain.
Direction is opposite to clamping, meaning entropy may increase.
Semantic memory is 𝐷 read directly, without a temporal index; episodic memory is the possibility field at a located past index, tethered to 𝐷.
Retrieval and the construction of a working arena are the same operation at different levels: both are sampling over slow structure.
Definition 3.14 (Readout).
Readouts are taken on the working arena, of the pushed-forward field 𝐸 𝑋 .
Two types are distinguished by what they take as input.
A probability readout is the mass of 𝐸 𝑋 over a region, and needs the field's shape.

A valence readout is a profile over the recruited coordinates, and needs its first moment: for each recruited coordinate 𝑖, where 𝑜 𝑖 is the origin supplied by one of the four sources of X1 and 𝐸 𝑖 is the marginal of 𝐸 𝑋 on 𝑖.
If 𝑔 𝑖 is constant over supp 𝐸 𝑖 (the ordinary case) this reduces to (𝜇 𝑖 -𝑜 𝑖 ) 𝑔 𝑖 with 𝜇 = 𝔼 𝐸 𝑋 [𝑥].
text.formatted: If 𝑔 𝑖 is constant over supp 𝐸 𝑖 (the ordinary case) this reduces to (𝜇 𝑖 -𝑜 𝑖 ) 𝑔 𝑖 with 𝜇 = 𝔼 𝐸 𝑋 <ref type="bibr">[𝑥]</ref>.

text.text: A derivation requiring a single signed reading uses a scalar combination over the profile.
Which combination is an algorithmic-level question and left open ( §3.6).
The AM commits to per-coordinate gain-weighted displacement, not to any rule for collapsing it.
For any magnitude readout, a compressive warp applies to the profile after the weighting, not inside it.
Thus curvature in a value function comes from the warp, while any kink comes from a sign boundary in 𝑔 (G2), allowing them to be manipulated apart.
Source attribution (that something really happened) is itself a readout, thus fallible [37].
text.formatted: Source attribution (that something really happened) is itself a readout, thus fallible <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">[37]</ref>.

text.text: Because a readout takes as input the pushed-forward field together with the origin compare reads against, both must be held fixed for a judgment to be unchanged.
A transformation Φ is judgment-neutral when it satisfies both of and Φ leaves the active origin unchanged.
The first stipulation says the transformation may move mass anywhere it likes among the collapsed dimensions, so long as nothing changes in the marginal the judgment actually reads.
The second says it must not relocate the standard.
The AM predicts that a judgment-neutral transformation has no effect whatsoever, and that any transformation failing either stipulation may have one.
This is the formal statement of the invariance requirement introduced in §2.6.
The whole marginal must be preserved, not just its first moment.
If a gain reverses across a dimension (G2), two distributions with the same mean and different shape read differently, so moment-matching is not sufficient.

The two stipulations are what the two kinds of readout take as input: a probability readout reads the marginal alone, so the first conjunct governs it; a valence readout reads the marginal against the origin (Def.
3.14), so it needs the second as well.
The pair is sufficient because nothing a readout takes as input is left free.
A coordinate carries a third component, its scale, but the scale's form is its constraint.
A pure rescaling leaves both quantities unchanged, since 𝑔 𝑖 carries inverse units and a region rescales with its coordinate.
Scale-invariance is a consequence of the condition, not an addition to it.
Definition 3.15 (Goal). goal ∶ (𝑅, 𝜏 > now) → clamp (𝐸, 𝑅) held at that index by 𝐴 with 𝑔 ≠ 0 somewhere on 𝑅, and drawing rent for as long as it is held.
text.formatted: Definition 3.15 (Goal). goal ∶ (𝑅, 𝜏 > now) → clamp (𝐸, 𝑅) held at that index by 𝐴 with 𝑔 ≠ 0 somewhere on 𝑅, and drawing rent for as long as it is held.

text.text: A goal is therefore an allocation-driven clamp; a point clamp is a desire, a path clamp is an intention.
Subgoals are intermediate states on low-cost paths, reached by backward spread along 𝑤, so goal hierarchy is encoded by path structure.
Progress is compare 𝑖 (clamp (𝐸, 𝑅), 𝑆).
Worth is the valence readout taken on the clamped region (Def.
3.14), whereas for a path clamp it is taken at the endpoint, since a route and its destination are worth the same and cost differently.
Competition, not threshold, releases a goal.
Threshold applies to allocationdriven clamps only.
Rent is a capacity quantity and worth is a valence reading, so they are not directly comparable (capacity forces an ordering).
When a competing demand cannot be funded, a held clamp is released.
The one released is always the cheapest to lose, which is the maintenance analog of the local stopping rule on traversal that §3.5 already licenses.
That ordering, which clamp is cheapest to lose, is a computational-level commitment.
How each clamp's worth (a profile, Def.
3.14) is collapsed to make the comparison is an algorithmic-level choice left open ( §3.6).
An input-driven clamp has a different fate: it is not held by 𝐴, draws no rent, and lapses with the input that set it.
An implication is that an externally imposed clamp cannot be budgeted away, so the two types come apart under load, such that an intrusive percept persists while a maintained goal is shed.
Two further consequences distinguish competition from a threshold rule.
A goal that has stopped paying does not lapse on its own schedule; it persists and intrudes until something else needs the capacity, which is the Zeigarnik pattern ( §4.4 and following).
Because rent scales with the region held while worth reads the endpoint, an intention under load degrades to a desire (the route is dropped, the destination kept) instead of being abandoned outright.
Because 𝐾 is treated as static over the episode (the timescale this account addresses), release runs only by competition.
A goal held in the absence of another one contending for the capacity has no route to release, which means that the account cannot drop a hopeless goal in a genuinely empty field.
This is the cost of the static-capacity bracket.
A depleting reserve would supply the internal adjustment beyond affordability needed to model commitments that persist past the point at which maintaining them stops paying.
I view that as a step up in modeling to the algorithmic level that belongs to an account of decision making, which can discipline the depletion and recovery rates against persistence data.
The substrate expresses values over a space.
Anything requiring a bound variable, or an argument that can be filled by different things, lies above it.
A bound variable is a slot, not a fact, and people will fill "what (blank) knows" with different, sometimes conflicting, content.
Reasoning about that content requires siloing the unique content of different people, including different versions of oneself.
The substrate represents content in a common space.
Maintaining your knowledge and somebody else's as sealed, conflicting states requires rolebased silos above that substrate.
Embedded attitudes, exact cardinality, nested quantification, relational and analogical mapping, and theory of mind lie above the AM.
The model specifies the interface to this layer and leaves its internal operations open.
Theory of mind can help illustrate the split: pointing the perspective index at another agent gives a shallow view of how it looks from there, which is something the arena can support.
Holding that agent's knowledge sealed off from one's own means maintaining a conflicting state nested inside the other's viewpoint.
That is a bound-variable operation (E6), and lies above the ceiling.
Local processes govern the AM.
Homeostasis sets 𝑔 over time (G5), resourcerationality motivates a local stopping rule on traversal, and coherence exerts local pressure over co-active contents [46].
text.formatted: Homeostasis sets 𝑔 over time (G5), resourcerationality motivates a local stopping rule on traversal, and coherence exerts local pressure over co-active contents <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">[46]</ref>.

text.text: Imposing any of these as a global objective would invert the direction of explanation on which the account depends.

The AM leaves a roster of functional forms open: the decay rate of activation, the sampling procedure in retrieval, the functional selecting the basepoint from 𝑆 𝑋 , the shape of the readout warp, the cost of maintaining a clamp, the learning rate on 𝑤, and the combination procedure at choice.
Evidence bearing on the last is often read as impacting accounts like the AM.
Whether a person integrates attributes compensatorily or scans them lexicographically [55, 69] is an algorithmic question.
text.formatted: Whether a person integrates attributes compensatorily or scans them lexicographically <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">[55,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">69]</ref> is an algorithmic question.

text.text: Evidence of strategy-switching under load [53, 54] constrains the choice of algorithm.
text.formatted: Evidence of strategy-switching under load <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">[53,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">54]</ref> constrains the choice of algorithm.

text.text: These open forms are algorithmic-level details left to later specification by design.
Between the primitives and the catalog entries sit composites, including constructed percepts like salience, value, fluency, felt-effort, felt-uncertainty, and surprise, among others.
They are derived but standing, meaning they recur across phenomena, are measurable as units, and are always assembled the same way.
Salience, the illustrating case, is activation allocated over 𝒳 by two dissociable recruiters, not read off the stimulus [2].
text.formatted: Salience, the illustrating case, is activation allocated over 𝒳 by two dissociable recruiters, not read off the stimulus <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref>.

text.text: Section 4.1 derives salience in full and contrasts it with value-distorting accounts.
This comparison is interesting because, for the AM, value is constructed for each judgment, never a retrieved preference ( §4.6).
It is the possibility field read out under drive-gain weighting, computed on demand and never stored.
The composite layer produces one recurring misreading: a middle-layer signal is taken to report a property of the world.
Retrieval fluency read as frequency yields availability.
The felt-closeness of an option read as its probability yields the conjunction fallacy.
The value percept read as a property of the object yields intrinsic value.
Trace-density read as truth yields the illusory truth effect [34].
text.formatted: Trace-density read as truth yields the illusory truth effect <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">[34]</ref>.

text.text: Phenomena, the JDM catalog entries, are found at the top AM layer.
They are the measurable, replicable regularities that are the arena model's target of explanation.
A phenomenon is derived when it follows from primitives plus operations without needing additional machinery.
They exist naturally at the top of the upward path that starts at the primitives and passes through the composites.

Some phenomena are direct copies of a composite, some are a composite misread as a property of the world (the template of §3.7), and still others fall out of the primitives and operations directly, with no standing composite in between.
The projection view gives the AM its primary reach: phenomena characterized by hidden-dimension artifacts.
Phenomena arising from capacity or noise, along with ecological adaptations scored against a mismatched standard, lie outside that view.
The AM's machinery can nevertheless handle some of them without dissolving them.
The arena model retrodicts a considerable portion of the JDM catalog.
The subset presented here serves as a consistency check.
Each entry provides a sufficient derivation; some admit multiple derivations using the same machinery.
When more than one process produces the same observed error, they typically disagree about what would make it disappear.
Experiments can test that disagreement, and the differing mechanisms allow an intervention to work in one case but not another.
I selected the cases because they are catalog entries that illustrate how the theoretical account alters interpretation.

My derivations follow the procedure in Appendix A. Each example locates two signals (the quantity the judgment warranted and the quantity it went on), identifies the worldly property that second signal is taken to report, and names the primitives that generate it.
Catalog entries not covered here can be located by the same procedure.
Dissolved, derived as misreading, handled, and resistant are the four core classifications made by the AM.
An entry is dissolved when judgment moves systematically along a hidden dimension, making the apparent error an artifact of the experimenter's basis.
The behavior is systematic within the full arena.
Other entries are derived as genuine, systematic misreadings during judgment: the operative signal is taken to report something it does not.
In those cases, the misreading is a fact about the path trace, and an applied standard supplies the error verdict.
Handled entries are real limits of cognition that the AM explains directly.
Resistant entries require an operation above the ceiling ( §3.4) and are handed off to another process.
Salience is a ubiquitous, recurring percept that biases attribution and judgment [68].
text.formatted: Salience is a ubiquitous, recurring percept that biases attribution and judgment <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">[68]</ref>.

text.text: Stepping through its derivation is good practice before engaging a canonical catalog entry.
The AM derives salience as the output of attention allocation: activation (𝐴) allocated over 𝒳, recruited by two dissociable inputs.
Stakes, the 𝐸-weighted drive-gain magnitude ‖ ḡ‖, captures how much is at issue -the movement in the grass when it might be a snake.

Precision demand draws activation to where the possibility field is inadequate: either because it is diffuse (high 𝐻[𝐸]), like a sound in the dark whose source is unplaced, or because its precision was just disconfirmed (high discrepancy), like a step that is not where the foot expected it.

When those two quantities are read as world-signals instead of being routed to attention, they become felt-uncertainty and surprise, standing composites of §3.7, thus attentional siblings to salience.
The derivation places salience in the structural class of entries: it is a composite between the fundamental judgment primitives and the proper phenomena of the catalog.
Importantly, salience and value dissociate because stakes recruit salience independently of value (G3).
This accommodates rumination, in which attention dwells on uncertainty while value remains constant.
The prominent behavioral economics view treats salience as attribute-level and value-distorting [7]: salient outcomes receive greater weight in valuation.
text.formatted: The prominent behavioral economics view treats salience as attribute-level and value-distorting <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7]</ref>: salient outcomes receive greater weight in valuation.

text.text: In contrast, the AM locates salience in attentional candidacy, which is independent of value by construction.
Two shapes of derivation appear below.
In template cases, a signal internal to the agent is read as if it were a property of the world, so the derivation names the composite being misread.
In direct cases, the substrate's own geometry surfaces, and the derivation names the substrate quantity itself.
The conjunction and availability examples are of the first kind, similarity asymmetry the second.
The classic example asks a person which of two options is more likely to be true: Linda is a bank teller or Linda is a bank teller and a feminist [71].
text.formatted: The classic example asks a person which of two options is more likely to be true: Linda is a bank teller or Linda is a bank teller and a feminist <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">[71]</ref>.

text.text: The compelling result is that people tend to select the latter, despite it representing a subset of the former.
The AM derivation of the conjunction fallacy is straightforward: 1.
Locate the signal.
A probability judgment reads 𝐸's mass over a region (Def.
The candidates are regions, not points: 𝑅 𝑇 (bank teller) and 𝑅 𝑇∧𝐹 (bank teller and feminist), with 𝑅 𝑇∧𝐹 ⊂ 𝑅 𝑇 .
Read as mass, regional containment strictly dictates the direction of the inequality (∫ 𝑅 𝑇∧𝐹 𝐸 ≤ ∫ 𝑅 𝑇 𝐸), so no conjunction can be judged more probable than its constituent conjuncts.
That is the warranted quantity, but it is not the operative one.
The operative signal is proximity: the per-candidate felt-closeness of Linda to a representative point, which is her typicality for that category, a readout of the cost-distance 𝑑 𝑤.
Identify what it is read as.
Each candidate is instead collapsed to a single representative point, which is the prototype of its cell (Def.
Collapsing a region to a point discards how much of the space it covers.
That size is precisely what made the conjunction rule hold.
Adding "feminist" moves the representative point closer to Linda, so proximity rises even as the required probability falls.
The misreading is not a noisier probability but a different quantity: proximity to a point substituted for the required mass over a region.
In other words, attribute-substitution [40] occurs because the mass of 𝐸 collapses to points.
text.formatted: In other words, attribute-substitution <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">[40]</ref> occurs because the mass of 𝐸 collapses to points.

text.text: The correct reading is a readout of the possibility field 𝐸.
The substituted reading is a warped readout of 𝑑 𝑤 , itself derived from the cost function 𝑤 (boundary condition Σ2), and the region-to-point collapse selects each candidate's representative point.
The substitution is cheap because 𝑑 𝑤 to a point is directly available, whereas mass over a region must be integrated.
Interventions that off-load the expensive readout, such as formatting information in a frequency format [13, 28], are effective because they make reading the regional mass of 𝐸 cheaper.
text.formatted: Interventions that off-load the expensive readout, such as formatting information in a frequency format <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[13,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">28]</ref>, are effective because they make reading the regional mass of 𝐸 cheaper.

text.text: The same coupling produces conversion errors in which "all A are B" is read as "all B are A." The directly available reading is the symmetric overlap of the two categories, but the asymmetric relation imposed by the AM would require traversing 𝑤 in the costly direction.
As in the conjunction, a cheap readout displaces an expensive one.
The difference is only in what gets collapsed: extent there versus direction here.
This aligns with mental modeling literature's claim that conversion errors rise under working-memory load [4, 38].

text.text: Availability.
People judge the frequency or probability of an event by how readily instances come to mind [72].
text.formatted: People judge the frequency or probability of an event by how readily instances come to mind <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">[72]</ref>.

text.text: A likelihood judgment should read 𝐸's mass over the region of instances (Def.
3.14), the same readout the conjunction requires.
The signal actually read is fluency: the felt ease with which instances come to mind.
Fluency is a standing composite, not the cost itself.
It is a compressive readout of retrieval cost, so that what is cheap to reach feels fluent.
It differs from true frequency: a single recent or vivid instance is highly fluent though rare.
Read as frequency, fluency inflates the estimate exactly when ease and frequency diverge.
Fluency is a warped readout of retrieval cost, that is, inverse traversal cost over 𝑤, with retrieval sampling along 𝑤 and tethered to 𝐷 (Def.
The correct reading is a readout of 𝐸; the substitution is cheap because fluency is directly felt, whereas mass over a region must be integrated.
The availability heuristic posits a mental shortcut.
The derivation is of the mechanism (ease of retrieval is what gets read when mass should have been), not of the shortcut.
The judgment is assembled from whatever instances happen to be sampled [67].
text.formatted: The judgment is assembled from whatever instances happen to be sampled <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">[67]</ref>.

text.text: Availability also illustrates a case of rival accounts disagreeing in a testable way.
The derivation just given treats the effect as a genuine misreading (fluency substituted for mass).
It predicts that the estimate can be corrected by making the set of instances explicit so that mass is read where fluency stood in.

The alternative account claims that there is no error: in natural settings, ease of retrieval tracks frequency, meaning reading one for the other is well calibrated, and the discrepancy surfaces only when a task decouples them.
This interpretation belongs to the ecological adaptations class of results that §2.5 sets outside of what the AM resolves.
The successor representation account makes the ecological route precise such that each state is encoded by its expected future occupancy, directly coupling accessibility and frequency [16, 26].
text.formatted: The successor representation account makes the ecological route precise such that each state is encoded by its expected future occupancy, directly coupling accessibility and frequency <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">[16,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">26]</ref>.

text.text: The two accounts predict different interventions.

The misreading account predicts that forcing an explicit reading of the instance set will remove the effect; the ecological account predicts that restoring the correlation between ease and frequency will remove it.
This disagreement is a testable consequence of applying the AM to the JDM catalog.
People judge "North Korea is similar to China" as truer than "China is similar to North Korea" [70]: the less prominent item is more similar to the prominent one than the reverse.
text.formatted: People judge "North Korea is similar to China" as truer than "China is similar to North Korea" <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">[70]</ref>: the less prominent item is more similar to the prominent one than the reverse.

text.text: Unlike availability and the conjunction, the warranted quantities and operative signals coincide.
Also, nothing is taken to report a property of the world.
The signal is read correctly, meaning that the derivation is structural.
Under the account, similarity is a readout of cost-distance.
Similarity is decreasing and compressively warped like any other magnitude read out (Def.

Because the cost function 𝑤 is directed, the induced 𝑑 𝑤 is a quasimetric (boundary condition Σ2: 𝑑 𝑤 (𝑎, 𝑏) ≠ 𝑑 𝑤 (𝑏, 𝑎), in general). "𝑎 is similar to 𝑏" reads 𝑑 𝑋 𝑤 (𝑎, 𝑏), the cost of reaching 𝑏 from 𝑎 on the working arena, and then reads it inversely, with what is cheap to reach being judged similar.
A prominent, high-𝐷 referent is cheap to reach from many starting points, while the reverse traversal is not, so the two phrasings read two different costs.
Another consequence of taking the readout on 𝑋 is that similarity shifts with the coordinates recruited.
That shifting accounts for the context-dependence and asymmetry Tversky famously documented [70].
text.formatted: That shifting accounts for the context-dependence and asymmetry Tversky famously documented <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">[70]</ref>.

text.text: Independent evidence for this form of similarity comes from the successor representation [16, 26], in which experience-dependent learning of directed transitions causes a peripheral state to sit closer to a central state than vice versa.
text.formatted: Independent evidence for this form of similarity comes from the successor representation <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">[16,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">26]</ref>, in which experience-dependent learning of directed transitions causes a peripheral state to sit closer to a central state than vice versa.

text.text: The effect is anomalous only against the assumption that similarity must be symmetric.
The directedness of 𝑤 is fixed by the possibility field's forward and backward structure (E4, E5), independently of anything about similarity, so the effect is predicted rather than accommodated.
Generativity, a core feature of the account, means the field can have mass in a region without input support (see E2).
This feature makes prediction and anticipation possible.
Unconstrained generativity can also produce pattern over-detection, that is, the perception of structure in its absence.
At least five catalog entries hinge on this same mechanism: • Apophenia: the tendency to perceive meaningful patterns, connections, or intent in unrelated data [12].
text.formatted: At least five catalog entries hinge on this same mechanism: • Apophenia: the tendency to perceive meaningful patterns, connections, or intent in unrelated data <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12]</ref>.

text.text: • Pareidolia: a specific type of apophenia: seeing or hearing familiar images or sounds in random sensory stimuli [64, 48].
text.formatted: • Pareidolia: a specific type of apophenia: seeing or hearing familiar images or sounds in random sensory stimuli <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">[64,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">48]</ref>.
