text.formatted: • Clustering illusion: perceiving a pattern in a small sample drawn from a random distribution <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">[29]</ref>.

text.text: • Hot-hand fallacy: believing a streak of success raises the odds of further success on the next attempt [30].
text.formatted: • Hot-hand fallacy: believing a streak of success raises the odds of further success on the next attempt <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">[30]</ref>.

text.text: • Texas sharpshooter fallacy: treating a cluster found after the fact as if it were a pattern predicted in advance [31].
text.formatted: • Texas sharpshooter fallacy: treating a cluster found after the fact as if it were a pattern predicted in advance <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">[31]</ref>.

text.text: The AM claims that these, along with anticipation and prediction, are all products of generativity, not rival faculties.
The dual-process account of cognition [20], colloquially "thinking fast and slow" [39], is one of the most recognizable JDM meta phenomena.
text.formatted: The dual-process account of cognition <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">[20]</ref>, colloquially "thinking fast and slow" <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">[39]</ref>, is one of the most recognizable JDM meta phenomena.

text.text: Its fast, intuitive process operates with little or no conscious effort or sense of voluntary control.
Its contrasting slow, deliberative process handles effortful and conscious mental operations.

The core determinants of the fast or slow trade-off map directly to AM components: cognitive load, stakes, and framing map to capacity availability (𝐾 minus current ‖𝐴‖ 𝐾 ), norm of the drive-gain vector (‖ ḡ‖; G3), and the working arena recruitment (𝑋).
The AM treats fast processing as the default because gain limits traversal through a local resource-rational stopping rule.
Slow processing draws on capacity in three ways: deeper sampling before readout, more coordinates maintained at once, and longer clamp chains (derivations).
These draws are separately measurable and may dissociate.
A single quantity that made them covary would restore the "fast and slow" dichotomy and falsify the AM's decomposition.
The account aligns more closely with judgment-as-a-spectrum [52] and bounded-rationality [65] accounts.
text.formatted: The account aligns more closely with judgment-as-a-spectrum <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">[52]</ref> and bounded-rationality <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">[65]</ref> accounts.

text.text: The AM classifies some catalog entries as handled: real cognitive costs that its machinery explains directly.
An uncompleted goal is a region of 𝐸 clamped at a future index and maintained at rent against capacity (Def.
While the clamp holds, it continues to draw on 𝐾, so interrupted tasks remain accessible and intrude, producing the Zeigarnik effect [75].
text.formatted: While the clamp holds, it continues to draw on 𝐾, so interrupted tasks remain accessible and intrude, producing the Zeigarnik effect <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">[75]</ref>.

text.text: Completion releases the clamp, after which the elevated accessibility decays.
Where Lewin posited a tension that holds the goal active, the AM derives its persistence from maintenance rent under the capacity constraint.
The AM claims that value is read-out valence, much like decision by sampling [67] and query theory [36].
text.formatted: The AM claims that value is read-out valence, much like decision by sampling <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">[67]</ref> and query theory <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">[36]</ref>.

text.text: In contrast, many choice models represent preferences with a utility function over outcomes.
For the arena model, value is a percept.
It is found in the middle layer, computed on demand, and personrelative.
When it is read as a property of an object, it becomes "intrinsic value."
This process amounts to naive realism about the value readout, making it a real, derived misreading during judgment.
The same move appeared in §2, where a rationality yardstick was treated as a property of the world.
This misreading occurs whenever a constructed, agent-relative readout is treated as a recov-erable fact.
Recognizing the value readout as agent-relative makes intrinsic value subjective.
Because each judgment constructs value anew, preference instability can arise across judgments.
The substrate does not support a bound variable ( §3.4).
Estimating what another person, or your past self, knows means filling that "knower" slot with someone whose knowledge differs from yours and keeping it quarantined.
Also, the substrate is not sealed, so your current knowledge can leak in.
Consider the curse of knowledge: a better-informed person is unable to disregard or "un-know" their private information when predicting the mental state of another [11].
text.formatted: Consider the curse of knowledge: a better-informed person is unable to disregard or "un-know" their private information when predicting the mental state of another <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[11]</ref>.

text.text: Their own knowledge leaks into their representation of the lessinformed person's.
Similarly, the hindsight bias happens when an individual falsely overestimates, in retrospect, how predictable an outcome was before it occurred [21].
text.formatted: Similarly, the hindsight bias happens when an individual falsely overestimates, in retrospect, how predictable an outcome was before it occurred <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">[21]</ref>.

text.text: In its case, present knowledge leaks across time into a person's representation of their past self.
The two differ only in which index carries the displacement, the perspective index 𝜋 for another person, the temporal index 𝜏 for a past self.
However, both need the sealing operation the flat indices (E6) cannot provide.
The possibility field can accommodate another viewpoint, but it cannot nest and seal inside that viewpoint a knowledge state different from one's own.
Performing that seal is a bound-variable operation, and that lies above the ceiling.
Half of each bias directly follows from this constraint.
With no seal, one's current knowledge leaks into the attempted simulation, whether across persons or time.
Per the AM, the self-to-other flow is why the error always runs toward what one already knows, and grows under load.
The other half does not follow from the constraint: performing the seal is the bound-variable operation itself, and there is no route to it within the AM.
The judgment process can only hand off to a theory-of-mind mechanism above the ceiling [32].
text.formatted: The judgment process can only hand off to a theory-of-mind mechanism above the ceiling <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">[32]</ref>.

text.text: Because the task is to model another mind, that hand-off is constitutive, not optional.
The AM specifies the interface at which it occurs.
The trigger is an algorithmic question for future work.
The entry is resistant for a stated structural reason: the path trace reaches the ceiling in need of the sealing operation.
This is a declared limit of the AM.
A defect would instead arise from absorbing the entry by retrofit or leaving an inconsistency unexplained by either a hidden dimension or a capacity cost.
Curse of knowledge exposes this boundary and makes the ceiling empirically meaningful.
The previous section was a consistency check covering the account's ability to derive, dissolve, and handle existing entries in the JDM catalog.
This section demonstrates the account's generative capacity through invariance predictions.
Traditional JDM studies propose a mechanism, find a manipulation, and report a difference, leaving null results ambiguous ( §2.6).
An invariance prediction sets a stricter criterion: an observed difference when none should exist undermines the account.
Gigerenzer and Hoffrage's frequency-format result for Bayesian reasoning provides a precedent for such a theory-derived null prediction [28].
text.formatted: Gigerenzer and Hoffrage's frequency-format result for Bayesian reasoning provides a precedent for such a theory-derived null prediction <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">[28]</ref>.

text.text: The AM extends this strategy across the catalog by asking of every entry, "what dimensions does the working arena recruit?"
Its central prediction is that a transformation along an unrecruited dimension leaves judgment unchanged.
Recall that the working arena (𝑋, Def.
3.3) is spanned by the dimensions a person recruits during a given judgment.
A readout takes as input the possibility field as it appears on that arena together with the origin that the compare operation reads against.
A judgment-neutral transformation preserves both.
New information confined to an unrecruited dimension moves mass along a collapsed coordinate while preserving the read marginal and active origin, so judgment remains constant.
A paraphrase that preserves the recruited basis and active origin has the same result.
By identifying effect-free transformations, this prediction exposes the account to rebuttal.
Boundary conditions X1-X3 specify the permitted dependencies of recruitment.

An observed difference under a transformation committed to in advance as judgment-neutral falsifies one of three things: the recruitment claim, the claim about which origin is active, or the neutrality of the transformation.
These commitments must be named in advance and remain fixed after the result is observed.
The framing example from §2.6 makes this concrete.
The account separates dimension framing (choosing which features to discuss) from valence framing (viewing a single feature as a gain or loss relative to a baseline).

Famous demonstrations, such as survival versus mortality rates, conflate the two mechanisms: reversing the dimension under evaluation automatically shifts its origin, leaving their contributions to the observed effect confounded.
The AM adds a prediction for shifts along dimensions outside the working arena: such shifts produce no framing effect.
The AM dissects deliberation into three separable draws on a single budget: sampling depth, coordinate breadth, and derivation length ( §4.4).
This decomposition differs from unidimensional accounts of a deliberative "system-2" and general-intelligence treatments of deliberative ability [20, 66].
text.formatted: This decomposition differs from unidimensional accounts of a deliberative "system-2" and general-intelligence treatments of deliberative ability <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">[20,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">66]</ref>.

text.text: Because the three draws share one budget, some covariation under load is expected.
Their independence nevertheless predicts differential sensitivity: each targeted load should primarily impair a different draw.
A deadline truncates sampling from 𝐷 before readout (Def.
A concurrent capacity load pushes against the ‖𝐴‖ 𝐾 ≤ 𝐾 bound and reduces the number of coordinates maintained (K2, Def.

text.text: An interruption collapses intermediate subgoal steps held at rent (K3, Def.
Crossing the three manipulations with the three draws produces a 3 × 3 design in which the primary impairment should differ by condition.
A single scalar measure of how "slow" a judgment was cannot capture that pattern.
An identity, such as scientist or cyclist, is not a recruited dimension but a cell (Def.
3.2), that is, a category with a prototype, which enters the account as a region.
Making an identity salient places an allocation-driven clamp on that region (Def.
3.11), which draws maintenance rent ‖𝐴| 𝑅 ‖ 𝐾 for as long as it is held (K3).
The AM already uses this mechanism for an uncompleted goal and the Zeigarnik effect [75]: a goal is an allocation-driven clamp (Def.

text.text: 3.15), and a held clamp is capacity spent, hence capacity unavailable elsewhere.
Membership effects are, accordingly, cue-recruited (the clamp is set by a cue), trace-densitydependent (the cell is a mode of 𝐷, Def.
3.2), and capacity-limited (the clamp draws on 𝐾).
Because 𝐾 is a single scalar reservoir (K4), an active identity never "lives rent-free."

It draws rent in competition with every other demand on 𝐾, such as another salient identity, a maintained goal, or any of deliberation's draws (sampling depth, coordinate breadth, and derivation length; §4.4).
The formalism produces two related predictions.
First, suppression is graded: rent scales with the region held, so a broader or more strongly maintained identity suppresses concurrent demands more.
Second, suppression is reversible: competition sheds a clamp when a rival demand exceeds the available capacity, and releasing the clamp returns that capacity in full under the fixed 𝐾 (K3).
Priming an identity should degrade an unrelated concurrent task measurably and reversibly, in proportion to the rent its region commands.
The shared budget applies equally to social and non-social content, making cross-domain crowding-out diagnostic.
If priming "scientist" and priming "cyclist" draw equal rent, they should impair a third, unrelated task equally; if one region commands more rent, it should impair that task more.
Crowding-out confined to identity-related tasks would undermine the shared-budget claim.
This mechanism has a direct empirical precedent.
Priming a self-relevant negative stereotype is shown to reduce working-memory capacity, and the reduction is shown to mediate stereotype threat effects on performance [60].
text.formatted: Priming a self-relevant negative stereotype is shown to reduce working-memory capacity, and the reduction is shown to mediate stereotype threat effects on performance <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">[60]</ref>.

text.text: The AM interprets that as a maintained, self-relevant identity concern drawing on a shared resource and thereby degrading an unrelated task.
That is the clamp-rent prediction of this section shown in existing data. 2
text.formatted: That is the clamp-rent prediction of this section shown in existing data. <ref type="foot" target="#foot_1">2</ref>

text.text: Choice tracks the drive-gain-weighted profile, not raw attribute magnitude.
When a dimension's gain is near zero, valence barely responds no matter how large the attribute grows (G3).
Consequently, only an intervention that changes the allocation of drive-gain weight will flip choice.
Two manipulations emerge from this feature of the AM.
First, hold 𝑔 (see Def.
3.7, G3) fixed and inflate an attribute on a gain-gated dimension (one identified as low-gain in advance by the stakes reading (G3), not by the null it is about to produce) as far as you like.
The AM predicts choice will not change, a property that holds regardless of the algorithmic implementation because a gated contribution stays negligible under any combination rule.
Second, hold the attribute values fixed, but shift 𝑔 by manipulating, for example, satiety.
The AM predicts that choice will flip.
The first manipulation targets the world (attribute magnitude), whereas the second targets the agent (drive-gain).
To ground this prediction, hold a snack fixed and inflate its rating on a nondominant dimension, such as the spiciness of a tortilla chip.
Choice should remain unchanged.
Holding the attributes fixed while manipulating hunger changes 𝑔 and should permit choice to flip.
A fixed-parameter weighted sum misses this asymmetry because both its weights and attributes remain unchanged.
A state-dependent utility model could capture the flip through refitting; the AM locates the state-dependence in 𝑔, a separately measured channel.

The paired manipulations address the question of whether 𝑔 governs choice independently of whether the readout is implemented through lexicographic scanning, compensatory integration, or another algorithm.
A means-state is more easily locked in when the superordinate goal is a highentropy clamp.
A diffuse 𝐸 blurs the progress read against the actuality field (E4, Def.
3.15), so discrepancy registers slowly and a concrete subgoal with a crisp progress read draws capacity instead.
Temporal distance is the most direct route to that entropy: E4 states that 𝐻[𝐸] grows with 𝜏-distance from the clamp.
Abstractness offers a second route.

When an abstract goal specifies a broader region of the possibility field (e.g., more states satisfy "be successful" than "submit the draft by 5pm"), 𝐻[𝐸] is raised by support-breadth, not the temporal extension.
This second route assumes construal-level abstraction maps onto support-breadth in 𝐸.
Because this mapping is not established elsewhere in this account, it is adopted here strictly as a working premise.

It also runs counter to the surface reading of the construal literature, on which abstraction strengthens superordinate control [24]; the AM instead bets that takeover tracks the entropy of the goal's target region, not the construal frame itself.
text.formatted: It also runs counter to the surface reading of the construal literature, on which abstraction strengthens superordinate control <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">[24]</ref>; the AM instead bets that takeover tracks the entropy of the goal's target region, not the construal frame itself.

text.text: Because the two routes to entropy are independent, they are cleanly dissociable: a proximal-but-abstract goal and a distal-concrete goal both elevate 𝐻[𝐸] through different machinery.

Crossing them yields a clean 2 × 2, and if takeover tracks entropy regardless of which route produced it, proximal-abstract and distal-concrete goals should show comparably elevated takeover relative to a proximal-concrete one.

The resulting pattern diverges from competing models: a single-route account (in which only temporal distance sets salience) would fail to predict it, as would a fixed hierarchy (which lacks an entropy parameter for either route).
A standard psychometric route to fitting a similarity metric is inferring a spatial representation from judged proximities: how similar people say two options feel [63].
text.formatted: A standard psychometric route to fitting a similarity metric is inferring a spatial representation from judged proximities: how similar people say two options feel <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">[63]</ref>.

text.text: Doing that well is straightforward because there is only one number to match.
The AM builds the metric differently, out of how costly it is to move from one option to another (𝑤 and the induced 𝑑 𝑤 ).
That transition is measured independently, through how long people take and how often they err (Def.
The cost-based metric should then reproduce the similarity ratings on its own with no need to fit it.
Agreement across the two measurement channels follows as a falsifiable prediction.
Consider two diagnoses with overlapping symptoms, bacterial pneumonia and viral bronchitis.
Under time pressure, a physician might hesitate between them or mix one up with the other.
Their response time lags and errors rise whenever a case sits near that particular boundary.
Those numbers, collected across many pairs of diagnoses, are what build the cost function 𝑤.

Because discrimination difficulty rises with proximity, pairs that are slow and errorprone to separate sit close and are assigned a low cost between them, while pairs the physician never confuses sit far and are assigned a high one.
From 𝑤 alone, the model derives the cost-distance 𝑑 𝑤 by chain closure (Σ2), and from 𝑑 𝑤 , a full ranking of how close every diagnosis sits to the others.
Separately, with no time pressure, the same physician sorts diagnoses into groups by how similar they seem, a casual similarity judgment, untouched by speed or error.
The AM predicts that the ranking built from triage mistakes should reproduce the groupings built from calm sorting.
It is deliberately ordinal: similarity is read through a compressive warp (Def.
3.14), which preserves order while allowing magnitudes to differ.
Because the two measures come from independent behaviors, their agreement is an empirical risk.
A mismatch between the diagnoses confused under pressure and those grouped together at leisure would falsify the AM; a directly fitted similarity metric does not face this cross-channel test. 3

text.text: The AM assigns experience to position instead.
Value is a 𝑔weighted readout taken on demand (Def.
3.14), so there is no cached quantity to go stale.

What experience writes is position: relocation in trace-density (𝐷) and cost (𝑤) is how an acquired taste or a practiced action is laid down. 𝑔's role is to process change in those structures, not to change itself (G5).
Learning cannot write to 𝑔 by construction.
The AM claims that drive state moves 𝑔 on a separate route and timescale, which is what allows for a shift in bodily state to re-value a cue without learning [59], a risky but testable commitment.

text.text: Using mere exposure, build a preference for a novel food, say anchovies on pizza, then satiate on that food's category (salty snacks) and re-test choice.

If the acquired preference is position in 𝐷, satiation should devalue the specific food exactly as it devalues any other category member, learned or not, because both are read through the same lowered gain.
The opposite is the AM's falsifier: the unlearned preference on that dimension drops while the acquired one holds.
The falsifier needs acquisition to write a stored, drive-independent gain forbidden by G5.
Conditioned taste aversion is itself a learned change in a food's worth [25].
text.formatted: Conditioned taste aversion is itself a learned change in a food's worth <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">[25]</ref>.

text.text: On the surface, that reads like learning writing to 𝑔.
The AM's interpretation is that aversion relocates mass onto a disgust dimension whose gain is already negative, not a sign-flip on the taste dimension.
That means the test above should devalue by satiety, and an aversion-devalued food should show disgustaxis recruitment instead of a reversed taste reading.
The AM prediction is in the nuance of cost.

The basic setup is to use instrumental conditioning to make an action serve a drive (reaching for a water bottle at your desk to stay hydrated), then satiate that drive (drink until no longer thirsty) and re-test choice of the action against an equally practiced alternative serving a different drive (checking email).
At moderate training the a direct measure of stable comparison cost [58].
text.formatted: At moderate training the a direct measure of stable comparison cost <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">[58]</ref>.

text.text: Moment-to-moment response time is shaped by fatigue, a recent cue, and alertness.
That momentary state has to be held steady, or accounted for, before the two measurements are truly comparable.

Recruitment must match too: because similarity is read on the working arena and shifts with the coordinates recruited, both tasks must recruit the same ones, or a disagreement reflects a shifted arena, not a failed prediction.
AM predicts satiation devalues the reach with thirst, which is what goal-directed responding does [1].

text.text: On its surface, that persistence appears to falsify G5.
The AM locates this persistence in recruitment (X1-X3).
Overtraining makes the action cue-driven, so the cue recruits the coordinates of the action while leaving the distal dimension served by the outcome collapsed.
Thirst is marginalized out by 𝑃 𝑋 .
Because valence is read only over the recruited gains (𝑔 𝑋 ; G3, Def.
3.14), a satiation-induced change to 𝑔 on the collapsed coordinate is absent from the judgment.
This is the same blindness the general form of invariances turns on: there the unrecruited coordinate carries a mass change; here it carries a gain change.
Persistence is a recruitment fact, which is why stress and time pressure, which push 𝛾 up the inverted-U and narrow recruitment (X3), tip behavior toward the habitual pole [61].

text.text: This interpretation relocates and sharpens the falsifier.
Widen the arena (remove time pressure, reduce arousal, or cue the served drive to recruit thirst (X3)), and the collapsed coordinate re-enters 𝑋.
The readout then consults the lowered gain, and devaluation sensitivity returns without requiring new learning.
A stored value would not recover: by construction, a cached quantity is value-blind and remains insensitive regardless of how broadly the arena is drawn.
The crucial test is whether an overtrained habit persists after the outcome dimension has been recruited.
If the reach survives full satiation in an arena that recruits thirst, while its goal-directed counterpart stops, then learning has produced a drive-independent value and falsified G5.
The mechanism by which overtraining collapses that coordinate remains an open algorithmic-level question ( §3.6); the computational claim locates persistence in recruitment.
Both routes test one claim, that experience relocates the state and leaves the gain landscape alone.
Either failing would independently break G5. 4

text.text: The arena model's small substrate regenerates much of the JDM catalog.
It does so by building upward from primitives through to the catalog entries.
The form this central result takes is what gives the arena model weight: the catalog's named entries do not each receive their own mechanism, but fall out of one compact set of primitives.
The arena model provides the support the projection view requires.

From its perspective, much of what JDM research files as irrationality is systematic motion along a dimension an experiment did not measure, or an internal quantity read as if it were a property of the world.
A bias, on this account, is not a defect bolted onto reasoning, but the shape a bounded system takes when it reads its own signals.
Two types of evidence support the arena model.
Section 4 provides a consistency check by showing how a small primitive set can account for much of the catalog.
This establishes the model's capacity to generate the catalog while leaving comparison with alternative accounts of individual entries open.
Section 5 demonstrates the central claim that the arena model is a falsifiable predictive tool that stakes itself on invariances and dissociations.
The provided examples are currently untested and open to scrutiny.
The arena model relies entirely on existing data; generating new empirical evidence is the objective of the broader research program.
Tempting as it is, I refrain from reporting a coverage percentage.
Any such figure would reflect subjective selection criteria masquerading as the model's actual reach.

Instead, coverage can be verified entry by entry using the procedure in Appendix A, and proportions across the three classes in Section 2.5 are ready for direct measurement, not only rough estimation.
The arena model is intended as a parsimonious account of human judgment, with parsimony assessed through structural dependencies.
The primitives divide the catalog according to dependence on the possibility field (𝐸).

Availability and the conjunction fallacy operate on fluency and cost-distance; their derivations invoke 𝐸 only to identify the warranted quantity that makes the substitution visible, while the readout remains determined by those operative signals.
Similarity asymmetry and conversion errors satisfy the stronger condition of independence from 𝐸 in both operation and derivation.
The parsimony claim rests on this stronger condition (Figure 1).
text.formatted: The parsimony claim rests on this stronger condition (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">1</ref>).

text.text: Crucially, the entries that neither take 𝐸 as an input nor invoke it form a clear, principled cluster -not a scatter of exceptions.
Magnitude and scaling effects follow directly from the compressive warp (Def.
3.14), relative-encoding effects stem from the directed structure of 𝑤, and similarity effects derive from 𝑑 𝑤 itself.
A primitive field invoked universally, without clear boundary conditions, would be unconstrained, absorbing whatever explanatory work is required.
By contrast, a field that specific catalog entries provably do not need demonstrates the true economy of a compressed account.
Three boundaries keep the account focused and falsifiable.
Scope ( §3.4).

The substrate expresses values over a space and specifies the interface to higherlevel operations involving bound variables, including nested perspectives, exact cardinality, and relational or analogical mapping.
The explicit criterion separating these levels contributes to the AM's falsifiability.
Dynamics ( §3.5).
The dynamics directly distinguish the arena model from the free-energy account introduced earlier.

Local processes govern the model: homeostasis only sets drive-gain over time (G5), resource-rationality supplies a stopping rule for traversal, and coherence supplies pressure over co-active contents.
A free-energy account begins with a global objective and works downward; the arena model begins with primitives and works upward to phenomena.
Level ( §3.6).
The account is pitched at Marr's computational level.

Several functional forms are intentionally left open for algorithmic specification: the decay rate of activation, the retrieval sampling procedure, the shape of the readout warp, the cost of maintaining a clamp, the learning rate on 𝑤, and the combination procedure at choice.
The account will advance along two axes: downward through Marr's levels, and across the cascade this project opens.
At the algorithmic level, open functional forms and choice procedures are empirically resolvable via simulation.
A faithful implementation should reproduce the derivations of §4 as emergent results.
A central design criterion here is sensitivity.
Primitives must couple such that small variations in capacity or gain yield large, structured behavioral divergence.
Too little sensitivity will cause artificial convergence; too much will produce pure noise.

Finally, the account's primary wager relies on a small, measurable tuning surface restricted to capacity, the gain profile (its shape together with its arousal modulation 𝛾), expertise-driven deviations in 𝑤, and experience-driven deviations in 𝐷.
The prediction is that population-typical priors and these few parameters will generate rich behavioral variety through their interaction.
The second axis follows the judgment and decision making trajectory: a model of judgment supports one of decision making, and intern the decision making model will support one of choice.

The AM limits supply targets for the next model: thresholding and commitment (how graded readouts become discrete states), response mode as a distinct operation (why one substrate yields a price, choice, or deferral depending on query format), and revision conditions beyond affordability (why commitments persist past the point of return).
Stated together, the predictions in §5 form a falsification register, that is, a list of outcomes that would undermine the arena model.
Some are more dangerous than others.

The model is at risk if (1) a transformation committed to in advance as leaving the recruited dimensions and active origin untouched nonetheless shifts judgment, breaking the claim that judgment reads only the recruited arena and its origin; (2) the three draws on deliberation prove nondissociable under targeted load, collapsing the decomposition back into the single dichotomy the account explicitly denies; (3) identity crowding-out remains restricted to social tasks, pointing to a dedicated module the account cannot accommodate; (4) choice changes when a gain-gated attribute is inflated with drive-gain held fixed, or fails to flip when drive-gain is shifted with attributes held fixed, breaking the claim that choice tracks drive-gain and not raw attribute magnitude; (5) proximal-abstract and distal-concrete goals fail to show comparably elevated takeover relative to a proximal-concrete goal, undermining the entropy account in favor of a single-route or fixed-hierarchy alternative; (6) the two channels of 𝑤 disagree, breaking the claim that error-speed inferences and direct similarity elicitation measure a single quantity; or (7) a preference learned through either acquisition route resists devaluation when the drive through which it was acquired is satiated, breaking G5's claim that experience relocates the state without writing a drive-independent value.
Together, these predictions make the model falsifiable and therefore useful.
The Arena Model is an attempt to give structure to the disjointed heuristics and biases catalog.
It argues that judgment runs on a low-dimensional projection of a higher-dimensional world.
This is the projection view, and it provides a theoretical foundation for a compact model that gives researchers a single, testable account as an alternative to the ever-growing JDM catalog.
The procedure in Appendix A is an invitation to apply the AM to catalog entries beyond those covered here.
The procedure specifies both the test and its failure condition.
The resulting regularities can be read either as a catalog of human error or as the consequences of reasoning with finite resources in an open world.
I hope you find the arena model compelling.
Like all models, it is wrong.
Like the foundational prior art it builds upon, it is a useful tool for understanding our internal worlds.
A select few entries are in the body.
This appendix gives the procedure to locate any other JDM catalog entry and assign to it what the account says about it, or show that it resists the model.
The conjunction fallacy in §4 is this procedure run in full; what follows states it in general.
Two quantities are at stake and both are required to locate an entry.
• The warranted signal: the quantity a judgment would have to read for the standard it is scored against to be met.
A probability judgment warrants the mass of the possibility field over a region; a value judgment warrants a valence readout.
• The operative signal: the quantity the agent actually uses.
This may be a cost-distance 𝑑 𝑤 , a trace-density 𝐷, a felt composite such as fluency, or the warranted quantity itself.
A difference between the two signals constitutes a substitution, typically driven by price: the operative signal is directly available, while the warranted one must be integrated.
Many familiar entries name, in ordinary language, the signal the agent is using, whereas the warranted quantity typically has to be read off the standard the entry is scored against.
Identify which property of the world the operative signal is taken to report.
Taking the operative signal for a fact about the object rather than a reading taken by an agent constitutes a reification.
The two gaps are distinct, and an entry may carry either, both, or neither.
Where a bias is present, it lives in one of the two.
Identify the primitives and operations that generate the signal.
If the path trace closes using machinery already specified, the entry is located.
If it closes only by introducing machinery for this entry, that is not a derivation but a retrofit, and should be reported as one.
If it does not close at all, proceed to the resistant case below.

A located entry has so far fallen into one of four kinds, separated chiefly by a single question: is a distal invariant at stake, a right answer that exists independently of how the problem is described?
• Dissolved.
No invariant is recovered, and the options judged "inconsistently" differ in a way the experiment did not measure, such as an unmeasured dimension or an origin placed differently.
The behavior is systematic motion in the full arena; the inconsistency is a projection artifact.
There was no misreading to score.
• Derived as misreading.
A signal is read as a quantity it is not.
Illustrations include a cheap readout standing in for an expensive one, or an internal quantity taken for a property of the world.
There was a misreading, and tracing it says why a sensible system does so.
• Handled.
The phenomenon is produced directly by bounded capacity, decay, or readout compression, not by being a cost-driven reading.
The distinction is needed because price also explains why a cheap readout displaces an expensive one, so a priced explanation cannot on its own place an entry here.
It is explained, but not explained away.
• Resistant.
The path trace does not close because the entry requires a bound variable (a nested perspective, a relational mapping, or an exact cardinality), which lies above the ceiling ( §3.4).
The account hands off in place of forcing a derivation.
An entry may instead belong to the conceded class of §2.5.
In that class, correct behavior is scored against a mismatched standard and the account claims no resolution.
Ultimately, the labels are bookkeeping in service of interpretation.
Traces are the "deliverables" of the model.

text.text: A worked case: Framing.
Take the framing effect in its canonical form.
Six hundred people are threatened by a disease.
Their situation can be described either as a number who will be "saved" or a number who will "die."
Across those framings, preferences reverse [73].
text.formatted: Across those framings, preferences reverse <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">[73]</ref>.

text.text: The principle it is taken to violate is invariance: alternative descriptions of the same outcome should yield the same choice.

The relative attractiveness of options, Tversky and Kahneman observe, "varies when the same decision problem is framed in different ways" [73, p. 457]: the same policy for six hundred lives, described as "200 will be saved" or as "400 will die" reverses stated preference.

3.8; the "saved" wording anchors at none-saved, the "die" wording at none-lost), so the two framings are read against different origins, using machinery already in place.
Classify: is a distal invariant recovered?
No; there is no groundtruth attitude toward the policy the judgment fails to return, so the reversal is systematic motion in the full arena, not an error.
The entry is therefore dissolved: invariance is false about the arena, not violated by the system, and the two descriptions coincide only in the experimenter's projection.
